record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study investigates safety-related neuron and channel roles using pruning and fine-tuning experiments, but it does not test the listed claims about single-job neuron poles, explanation faithfulness, or attribution-graph sufficiency.
record.gate_note: The paper reports neuron/channel role assignments based on pruning and their share of model units. These results are relevant to the broader idea of analyzing model behavior at the unit level, but they do not measure neuron-pole jobs or test explanations on held-out activations. The paper's safety-preservation results concern fine-tuning defenses, not the listed claim versions.
record.test_reason: The study assigns neurons/channels to safety, utility, both or neither roles via activation-variance pruning and measures benchmark effects. It never explains neurons, counts poles with one job, scores explanations on held-out text, or builds attribution graphs, so none of V1–V7 is tested. It does not cite the original sources; 'cites_only' or 'discusses' both overstate engagement, and T6 is correct.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors propose SSAH: safety alignment is an implicit binary fulfil/refuse decision relying on a small set of safety-critical neurons/channels. Freezing SCUs plus some CUs preserves safety under fine-tuning, and tuning only redundant units reduces alignment tax. They conclude the atomic functional unit for safety is at the neuron level; the appendix frames this as speculation.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses structured pruning based on activation-variance importance scores to assign safety, utility, shared, and redundant roles, then tests pruning and freezing effects. It does not use neuron-pole explanations or held-out explanation evaluation.
record.method_sensitivity: Results are reported across different models, safety and utility benchmarks, pruning ratios, fine-tuning datasets, and safety judges.

fits_no_version.finding: Under pruning attribution, most units (about 70–85%) are classed as Complex Units contributing to both safety and utility. Only about 1.3–2% are exclusively safety-critical. Fine-tuning moves more than 65% of SCUs into other roles.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Under activation-variance pruning attribution, most neurons/channels in 7–8B chat models contribute to both safety and utility, and few are exclusively safety-critical.

record.problems: The role assignments are defined by pruning-based performance effects on selected safety and utility tasks, not by testing whether human-readable neuron explanations generalize to unseen activations. The reported SCU proportions do not measure the fraction of poles with one job. No uncertainty estimates are stated for these proportions.
record.rows_left_out: Detailed pruning benchmark scores and fine-tuning attack/defense outcomes in Tables 1–17 and Figures 5–13 are left out because they report safety/utility performance or defense effectiveness rather than the listed neuron-interpretability outcomes.

untested.parts: No Qwen3-32B, no neuron-pole explanations, no job-count shares.
No interpretability shares across models or scale.
No vision models or polysemantic-neuron reanalysis.
No tool or architecture comparison of interpretable-neuron shares.
No attribution graphs or replacement-model comparisons.

record.verdict_notes: Relation changed to cites_only/none-tested in spirit. The study does not discuss the claim's interpretability questions. The 'Complex Unit' majority could loosely be read as neuron multifunctionality. However, it is defined by pruning sensitivity on two task sets, not by explained activation behaviour, so it should not be linked to V1/V2.

versions.untested_parts: The paper does not assess Qwen3-32B, neuron poles, single versus multiple jobs, or the share of poles that are not understood.
It does not test whether the claimed job shares hold across models or scale, including mixture-of-experts or trillion-parameter models.
It does not examine InceptionV1 cat-and-car neurons, pose, or recursive generalization.
It does not test architecture, regularization, tool quality, or the stated estimates for interpretable neurons in vision models.
It does not build attribution graphs or evaluate behavioral explanation, replacement models, or reconstruction error.
It does not test explanations against activation locations on examples beyond those used to write them.
It does not score automated neuron explanations by simulating activations on new text.
